speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. Last evening the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) participated in a broadcast outside the house about a matter being discussed in the house, namely the Currie report. I, of couxse, take no exception to that action. However, in the broadcast the hon. member used these words:
But at any rate may I also point out that the Prime Minister himself, back in 1945, received certain documents which he knew were stolen.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO RADIO BROADCAST BY MR. KNOWLES
speechtext: What do you mean by that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REFERENCE TO RADIO BROADCAST BY MR. KNOWLES
speechtext:
The documents that Igor Gouzenko brought to him when he was minister of justice and he felt it in the interest of the state that use should be made of those documents even though he knew quite clearly whence they had come.
I do not doubt that the hon. gentleman's recollection of what took place in 1945 may have become a bit hazy, but that statement is quite untrue. I never at any time saw Igor Gouzenko nor his documents nor did I at any time have them in my possession. The whole story is related in quite some detail by the then prime minister in Hansard of March 18, 1946, starting at page 47. I will not take the time of the house to read it but any hon. member who wishes to refresh his memory about the complete details will find them enumerated there. In the report of the royal commission which was set up to inquire into that matter, in another long narrative of the facts he will also find the following paragraph at page 644:
Gouzenko, his wife and child, remained in apartment 6 for the rest of the night, under the care of the city police. There was a later caller at apartment 4 in the night but he retired in a short time without incident. On the morning of the 7th of September, Gouzenko was taken to the office of the B.C.M.P. where he turned over his documents, told his story and asked to be kept in protective custody as he feared for his safety and that of his wife and child.
My own. personal recollection of the facts is that on the morning of the 6th of September-parliament was opening on that day- I did not go to the Justice building but came directly to the centre block here, and that when I arrived here my secretary reported to
me that a man with his wife had gone to him and asked to see me and had explained that he wanted to see me because he was from the Russian embassy and had some papers that he felt were of importance to the security of Canada. I answered that I could not see him, that we were maintaining friendly diplomatic relations with the Russian embassy and that I could not take any part in any quarrel between an employee in the embassy and his employers. I felt that that might become a rather serious international incident.
I communicated with the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs and told him what my attitude had been and that, unless I received directions from the government to act otherwise, that is the way I felt I should act; that my secretary had a story that he would tell the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs if he wished to hear it. I heard nothing more about it that day or until an incident that afterwards I found rather amusing. The high commissioner for the United Kingdom was having a reception out at Earnscliffe. It was a fine day and he was receiving his guests on the lawn. I was standing chatting with him when the Russian ambassador came up to greet his host. I still stood there and we had a few minutes' conversation, in the course of which the high commissioner asked the ambassador-who, I gathered afterwards, used to do some fishing in the Ottawa river opposite Earnscliffe-if he had done any fishing recently. The ambassador had not done any in the last few days, and he turned to me with a smile and said: "And what about Your Excellency? Did you find the fishing good today?" Well, I did not know that he was chaffing me about the possibility of information having been conveyed to me by someone from the embassy. But afterwards I came to the conclusion that perhaps my sense of humour was not as keen as was that of the ambassador.
It will be recalled that this man had tried on the 5th to tell his story, and had told his story to someone in a newspaper office, and had not been taken very seriously. He had tried that day, or on the 6th of September, to get someone to take his story seriously and had failed to do so. He had then asked-being apparently in real fear for his security-the occupant of apartment six in the apartment house where he had apartment four if he

Currie Report
could not stay there, or if they would not take care of his child because he was afraid there might be some attempt to reach him in. his own apartment, and there was an attempt which is related in this report by the Prime Minister and related in the report of the royal commission that there had been a fracas there. Four people had burst into apartment four and had ransacked it. The municipal police had been alerted and they did appear on the scene, and they watched over Gouzenko and his family's safety during the whole of that night, and the next morning they took him to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I was informed that that was taking place; I was told that he was brought there by the city police. I said: "Well, that seems to be regular procedure. I am not giving any instructions to the R.C.M.P. to behave in any other way than they behave when incidents are brought to their attention by municipal police." After that, the thing developed, but to the best of my recollection I never at any time saw Gouzenko. I did not see him to know that he was Gouzenko even if I did happen to see someone going by with the R.C.M.P. who actually was Gouzenko, and I never saw the documents.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Argue, seconded by Mr. Wright, asked leave to make a motion under standing order 31 to adjourn the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. The motion is made according to the rules after the ordinary daily routine of business has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon. The motion is accordingly made at the right time. The hon. member has stated the matter and has handed to me a statement of the matter proposed to be discussed.
It is my duty is determine whether it is in order and of urgent public importance. I have read the motion. One question for me to consider is whether the matter is one of urgent public importance in accordance with the rules of the house. I should remind the house that the question of urgency is one which means that the matter is so important that the national interest would suffer if consideration of it is not proceeded with immediately. The provisions with respect to this matter are found in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, citation
114':

172 and following citations. Let me refer hon. members to citation 176, which reads:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the house may be moved under standing order 31, must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
And may I also remind hon. members of the second paragraph in citation 174, which reads:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
This is a matter which has been under consideration by a royal commission for some considerable time. The report of the royal commission was tabled yesterday. I am sure there will be ample opportunity within the near future, under the rules of the house, to discuss the matter. I do not feel it is one which should be debated today, so as to interrupt the business which has been arranged for today. Therefore I cannot allow the matter to be proceeded with at this time.

The house resumed, from Friday, January .6, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. laurent for the appointment of a committee o examine defence expenditures and com-nitments, and the amendment thereto of Mr. llaxton, and the amendment to the amend-nent of Mr. Knowles.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to intervene but briefly in his debate, which is taking place on the ubject as set forth in the resolution read to he house a moment ago by the Clerk Assisting Many matters have been covered in lebate, with some of which I should like to leal again. I do not think it would be fair o the house, however, to repeat some of the irguments made here before, important as hey may be.
References have been made to statements nade by the chief of general staff, both in a etter tabled in the house and in an article vhich has appeared subsequently in the Can-idian Army Journal. I was very glad indeed o hear the statement of the Prime Minister ^Mr. St. Laurent) that the article in question lad been written prior to the chief of general tail having seen the Currie report. This night suggest that the printing of the Canadian Army Journal is not as expeditious as >ne might like. Nevertheless it is a good hing that the statements contained therein annot be construed as a criticism of the louse of Commons, as such.
However, in his letter, the chief of general taff referred to what he termed as attacks

upon the armed services. And the minister, speaking in the house on January 13, said, as reported in Hansard'.
Perhaps I have been overenthusiastic In the defence of the armed forces, against what I felt to be unjustified charges.
I say, with respect, that that is a red herring thrown across the trail to try to obscure the real matter which should be investigated. In so far as I know, there have been no charges made against the armed forces at any time-certainly by no member on this side of the house. That should be made clear.
Mr. Currie in his report, and quite properly, reflects credit upon and compliments the members of the armed forces for having failed to walk through the open door which was left open to them by the administration, through this government, of the Department of National Defence. He says that it reflects great credit upon the honesty and integrity of the members of the forces. With that we all agree. We realize, as I think the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) said earlier in this debate, that in any group of men you are bound to find some crooks. That is true. But we do take pride in the fact that the number of those who have appeared in any investigation of the armed forces is very small indeed.
I am sure that the reputation of our armed forces as to either honesty or efficiency, will compare very well with the reputation of the forces of any other nation in the world. I am quite sure that members of the armed forces would compare most favourably with a similar group of citizens from any walk of life, even members of the House of Commons. Some of us have had experience in the armed forces. There are many sitting around here, some like myself, who were rear rank privates while others were colonels, generals or occupied comparable ranks in the sister services. I think we all realize that the one thing which undermines the morale of the armed forces more than anything else is the loss of confidence in those at or near the top. That is something which saps the morale of the armed forces. It is something this parliament should rectify. That is what we are trying to deal with during this discussion of the Currie report, and nothing more.
Let us analyse for a moment the speeches made by the Solicitor General and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), the latter speaking on January 13, both of which were long, both of which fully covered the field, and both of which were undoubtedly carefully prepared. I think they made the best defence possible in view of the circumstances with which they were confronted.

What do we find? I think their arguments fall into two classes. In the first place they both denied that there was any breakdown in the administration of the department. I think they denied that categorically. Then they went on to say, following somewhat the principle of the pleadings which were m effect under the old common law practice of confession and avoidance, that if there was a breakdown, which they submitted there was not, then it was due inevitably to the sudden expansion of the department brought about by the Korean crisis and the impossibility of getting trained personnel with which to perform the task confronting the department.
That is a most plausible explanation. It is one which perhaps we could understand, it is one which perhaps we could accept with some sympathy, if it were not for some of the statements which have been made by the Minister of National Defence in dealing previously with this matter. I have gone back through Hansard to look up some of the statements made by the minister with respect to the reconstruction of this department and its expansion. We remember in 1946 when the legislation was passed providing for the reorganization of the department following the war. Steps have been taken since then to develop this department.
We find that on June 24, 1948, almost five years ago, the minister, speaking on behalf of the government, set forth the purpose of the Department of National Defence, and I quote from page 5784 of Hansard of that date as follows:
(2) to provide the operational and administrative staffs, equipment, training personnel and reserve organization which would be capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need;
That was a program which the minister laid down for himself, for the government and for his department in 1948. On August 31, 1950, the minister summed up the work of his department during the past year and then went on to say, and I quote from page 104 of Hansard as follows:
In conclusion I think we can say that we have been fortunate in that we were able to complete-
I ask you to note the word "complete", -the post-war organization of the armed forces earlier and to a greater extent than most other countries, so that we have a sound organizational foundation upon which to build. It is, I believe, a smooth-working and efficient set-up-
Having reviewed his department during 1950, that was the statement made by the minister. Then during his estimates in 1951 there was some discussion with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), who inquired about the set-up. The minister is reported on page 3362 of Hansard of May
Committee on Defence Expenditure 24, 1951, as having replied to the hon. member for Greenwood as follows:
It is set up in accordance with the practice wmch has obtained in the Department of National Defence over the years. There has not been much change. We have to do a job, and we do it.
That was a summary given by the minister in 1951. In other words, in 1948 we have the minister setting forth the program which he has to accomplish, that is, the setting up of an administrative nucleus which could be expanded to meet any demands. In 1951 we have the minister boasting of the fact that that has been accomplished. That program was to cover an administration organization which would be capable of expansion to meet any demands, to use the minister's own words.
What do we now find? We find the minister and the Solicitor General coming into the house and saying, "It is true, we have run into difficulties, but that is because we have been expanding, it is because we have not been able to get trained personnel, it is because we have not the organization which we should have in order to meet the demands with which we are confronted." I think that one can say without being unfair that what the minister is saying is this: If we have failed, and we have failed to some extent, then our failure is due to the fact that we failed to set up the organizational set-up which we told the house we had set up. In other words, the house was not treated frankly when those questions were asked before and when the picture was created that we had a nucleus which could be expanded to meet any demands. Now we have failed because forsooth we failed in the past in setting up that organizational base.
In this connection I think one should point out that in 1947-48 this government spent for national defence in the establishment of this nucleus $239-9 million. In 1948-49 we spent over $252 million. In order to establish the nucleus which the minister said would be capable of expanding to meet any demands we spent over a quarter of a billion dollars in each of those years.
In 1936-37 this government spent $36 million through the Department of National Defence. Having spent what now appears to be a most paltry sum upon a nucleus for the defence of Canada, the Department of National Defence was able to expand and to take care of all the administration work entailed in fighting a second world war. According to the boasts of the government, they expanded it efficiently, there was no

Committee on Defence Expenditure scandal or no suggestion of waste or extravagance. Yet a few years later with an expenditure ten times as large they were not able to make the expansion which was so necessary to be made.
In that connection too I should like to refer to another statement of the minister to the non. member for Greenwood in the same debate on May 24, 1951. The hon. member for Greenwood had raised some question about the possibilities of moneys being wasted, and the minister said, as found at page 3348 of Hansard:
I should like to ask the hon. member who has just expressed these vague fears if he knows of any reason for having them. If he knows of any failure of the services engaged in inspection to do their job properly I should like to hear about it. I have not heard about it and therefore I can assure him that I know of no reason for expressing dissatisfaction with the present situation. I hear of all cases that involve trouble, and I have heard of no case.
That is the statement of the minister to the hon. member for Greenwood in May of 1951. Yet Mr. Currie in his report refers to the fact that the chief auditor had made reports time and time again. Mr. Currie said:
Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from appendix "B" which summarizes his findings over a period of years. The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
We have the situation that in May, 1951, the minister said he had heard no report whatsoever reflecting on matters concerning his department. Yet we have this unqualified statement in the Currie report speaking about report after report that had been referred and pigeonholed. The minister did not deal with this matter in his lengthy address the other afternoon. I think the minister should tell the house whether he obtained these reports to which Mr. Currie refers. If he did not get them, why did he not get them? If he did get them, why did he make a statement such as he made to the hon. member for Greenwood in reply to his question? I think those are matters with which we are concerned.
The minister did say that some time in February of 1952, I think it was, a committee was set up, almost a tri-service committee, representing the Auditor General, his own department and others, to conduct an investigation. He says that at that time he had received reports about Petawawa and other matters and he set up an investigating committee to conduct an inquiry. I wonder

if that was the first investigation that was conducted for the department? I wonder it the minister received no other reports before that. He was laying the foundation for the expansion of his department. Would he not apply to the civil service commission, for instance, for administrative personnel when necessary? Would there not be reports by officers of the civil service commission with respect to his department? I wonder how many reports the minister did receive concerning affairs in his department. I wonder if, for instance, he received reports criticizing construction costs. We have had a statement by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) respecting certain defence costs. I wonder if reports were received showing that buildings constructed by the engineers, for example, cost twice as much as those built by civilian contractors long before 1951. How many reports, if any, other than this one which the minister received, were received by his department, if not by him, prior to May 24, 1951?
Those are matters concerning which I think the house is entitled to more information than it has received heretofore. I quite agree with the minister that we are not concerned here with looking for scapegoats, and whatever our own interests may be in this house, certainly the people of Canada are not concerned with us playing politics. What they want is the situation cleared up so that the defence department and armed services can be maintained at as high a standard of efficiency as possible, and so that the taxpayers' dollar, 50 cents of which goes into this department, can and will be safeguarded. It is for that purpose that the defence expenditure committee is being set up, and f do not think it is fair to the committee to hamstring it by an order that it must first deal with the Currie report. In other words, the function of the committee would then be to investigate the investigator.
There are many other things that should be investigated by the committee. There are tremendous expenditures of government money concerning which the people expect a report by this parliament. Normally the house will be rising in a few months, and with the vast amounts of money that have been expended by this department and which expenditures have been referred to the committee, I say, sir, that it is not expedient, practical or right that the committee should be compelled to deal first with the one matter of this report and therefore be precluded from investigating many other matters with which the committee would like to deal. In fact it would appear that not only is the government attempting to becloud the matter of the Currie report itself, but by tying it in with

this committee it is also going to do its best to hamstring that committee and prevent it from conducting investigations into other matters which certainly should be investigated rather than the one question of the Currie report.
I do not intend to go further into this subject at this time. I think it is a matter of paramount interest to the nation, and one with which parliament should deal and deal now. I should like to make one reference to a matter which transpired yesterday and which possibly is sub judice now. However, I intend to make no specific reference except to the letter tabled yesterday by the Attorney General of Canada having to do with certain investigations and saying that following normal police practices certain matters had been referred to an individual. Without going into the details of any one matter, I wonder just what the reference to "normal police practices" means. We have heard a reference this afternoon by the Prime Minister to the police dealing with a national matter threatening the safety of the state and on a national basis. I have had some little experience with police matters as a prosecuting officer for many years and sometimes as defence counsel, and it is my experience that it is not the function of the police to conduct investigations on the orders of the Attorney General of Canada and then apparently to pass the matter on to an individual and say, "Either you deal with this or not", with the inference that if you do not you are failing in your duty to the state.
If there is a crime under the provisions of the Criminal Code, that is a matter for the attorney general of the province, and with that he should deal. If there is no crime under the Criminal Code and if it is a matter affecting the safety of the state, then it is one with which the Attorney General of Canada should deal as attorney general and not simply table correspondence in the house saying that the matter has been referred to an individual, and will he now please make up his mind what he is going to do about it. I doubt if that is consistent with the way in which matters of this kind should be dealt with, and I think it is something which will cause concern to all who do not want to see the intervention of police in matters which at one moment are termed criminal and at another moment savour of a political investigation. These, sir, are simply some observations of many that could be made on this report at this time.

The amendment of the Minister of National Defence was to instruct the committee-

Then, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a C.C.F. member, moved:
-to give consideration to the desirability of recommending that Mr. Currie be asked to conduct a further inquiry into any other expenditures and commitments covered by the terms of this resolution.

It was well known to the government that in our opinion there was no need for the Currie report to go before the committee on defence expenditure; it was well known to the government that we asked only for action on the Currie report, but that we did seek a wider inquiry into the broad field of organization and administration of the Department of National Defence which it was obvious should take place because of the disclosures in the Currie report.
I am speaking at this time on the first occasion in this debate. I have waited in the hope that there would be some indication from the government that it would accept the suggestion which I made directly in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on December 18 and which has been repeated on other occasions since then, that there be an inquiry into the broad details of organization and administration of the Department of National Defence. It is clear now, however, that the government intends to proceed with the course which it stated it intended to follow at the time that its position was put forward on the evening of December 17 last. Because of the extent to which an attempt has been made to divert attention from the real considerations before us I think it may be well to clarify some of those issues.
In the statement made by the government on the evening of December 17 an attempt was made to belittle the importance of the Currie report. Furthermore, an attempt was made in that carefully prepared statement by the government to create the impression that any attempt to deal with the disclosures in that report was to be regarded as an effort to take political advantage from the situation disclosed. In addition, it was indicated that the government proposed to divert attention in any way it could from the seriousness of the situation for which, as a government, it must accept full responsibility at this time.

The thing which it seems necessary to repeat and to emphasize is that the Currie report deals only with a very small segment of one part of the army, and deals in no way with the air force, the navy, or with any of the remaining parts of the army not covered by the direction to inquire into the army works services of the engineers. When these fantastic irregularities are disclosed within that small segment, then is it within the bounds of reason to suggest that the breakdown in the department which permitted that to happen affected just one small part of the army? If any argument of that kind were to be made, the answer to that argument was furnished to hon. members of this house by the annual report of the Auditor General tabled here a week ago yesterday. That report, presented by an official whose integrity and independence is unchallenged and unchallengeable, indicated that there are eight different methods of accounting within the Department of National Defence.
Do not let anyone come before this house and suggest that this is a desirable system, and one which has been maintained because of its efficiency. The Auditor General makes it perfectly clear that the ineffectiveness of the system has been emphasized over and over again, and that the government has failed to take the appropriate action to bring about the single system of accounting which is desirable.
These truly fantastic irregularities reported in the Currie report, almost all of which occurred in one camp, were under one system of accounting. What of the other seven systems? What is the evidence in regard to them? The Auditor General makes it quite clear that those other systems are not working any better.
He reports, as an example, that a brigadier in the army, proceeding to the civilian branch of the same service, receives a large salary in that office immediately upon his appointment to the civilian post, and for three months thereafter received the large salary paid him in the civilian post and at the same time his salary or pay as a brigadier. Other examples were given of irregularities which this chaotic system of accounting had permitted.
And yet, after this length of time, since the Currie report was presented to the house- now more than a month ago-there has not been any attempt to apologize to the house and, through the house, to the people of Canada, for the condition which has been disclosed. Committee on Defence Expenditure an exaggeration of the importance of the situation or, on the other hand, an attempt to create uncertainty in the public mind as to what the situation really is.

This Currie report brought before us for consideration, by the amendment presented by the government a week ago today, is a symptom of a grave disease, not the disease itself. By the introduction of the Currie report in relation to the defence expenditure committee the government itself has placed squarely before us its administration of national defence. Has the government instructed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to conduct an inquiry as to who got a copy, in advance, of the report of the commission inquiring into the prospects of the South Saskatchewan power and irrigation development? Certainly one report was just as confidential as the other-but there is a difference, remember. There is a difference. The report on the South Saskatchewan development was a report to the government, and if it got out here in Ottawa it got out from the government and not from a printing office in Montreal or in Regina or in Saskatoon. Perhaps the government in this case feels that as long as it is theft from the government it is a kind of selective theft to which there is no objection. But let us make no mistake about it: if one was reprehensible, the other was. If the removal of one paper was open to criticism and justified an inquiry by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, so did the other.
Now, do not let anyone suggest that there was no criticism of the leak of information in that other report. Perhaps, as a matter

Let me mention another matter dealt with in that report. It is under the subheading "Failure in Security". These are the words of the Currie report in that respect, as found at page 715 of Hansard:
There was in addition a serious collapse in security. There was little to prevent or to detect the organized plundering of military stores on a systematic scale, though apparently comparatively little of it took place. If there is excuse'for inefficient accounting, there is none for the failure of security which is, after all, a prime military consideration. I take a serious view of this breakdown. If it is easy to pilfer military stores, then, by the same token, it is easy to sabotage military equipment.
That is the most important single statement in this report. I refer to the statement that as a result of the breakdown in security, of the general inefficiency of this department in its supervision of army stores, there is the possibility not only of pilfering and looting but also of sabotage of military equipment.
We now come to the suggestion that this report which has been tabled be submitted to further inquiry, and that is the substance of the amendment which the government has introduced. Why is a further inquiry now needed into that part of the army activities already covered by the Currie report? Let us remember that, at the time Mr. Currie was appointed, the committee on defence expenditure was then meeting and could have dealt with this subject, as is now suggested. The government chose another course. The government decided that this was a subject that could be better dealt with by an independent inquiry carried out by Mr. Currie. On a number of occasions the defence expenditure committee was told that it could not explore certain subjects because of that fact.
Let us see what the government thinks about the reliability of this man whom they chose to conduct an alternative type of inquiry. At pages 1814 and 1815 of Hansard of May 2 of last year this statement was made on behalf of the government by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) in regard to Mr. Currie:
I announced the appointment of Mr. George S. Currie, a prominent chartered accountant and a man of outstanding integrity . . .
Mr. Currie had been deputy minister of national defence. He had served with distinction in the first world war and we felt that no better man could be found to do this job if we searched the length and breadth of the country.
That was referring back to the statement made by the minister on behalf of the government on April 21, and emphasizing their complete confidence in Mr. Currie's ability and integrity. We now have the report by this extremely able man. What earthly purpose can there be in submitting this report

of one inquiry to another inquiry? This report and the report of the Auditor General make it clear that what we need in this case is not a further inquiry but action; and that what we need in the way of inquiry is a similar one to be conducted by Mr. Currie into the rest of the army and the whole of the navy and the air force with regard to organization and administration by the Department of National Defence.
We have been told by Mr. Currie that so lax were the methods used that there was an invitation to wrongdoing. That invitation has been extended by these lax methods right across Canada. Surely what all of us want to see is the removal of any possibility that these lax methods may continue. The best way that can be done is to have a complete and comprehensive inquiry into the whole of the Department of National Defence, as has been suggested.
Mr. Speaker, when the proposal is put forward that there be an inquiry of this kind, the most improper statement has been made that this proposal constitutes criticism of our armed forces. I cannot imagine anything less worthy of this government than the suggestion that an attempt to deal with this situation constitutes criticism of the armed forces. Every remark I have made is directed to the government. The one place where criticism should be directed is to the government itself for the conditions which existed and the invitation, as Mr. Currie states it, to wrongdoing, which has been created right across this country.
And not to the thieves.

Mr. Speaker, when interjections of this kind and suggestions such as those to which I have referred are made, I remind those who make them that the hon. member who spoke first was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). When these statements are made about the criticism of the army and the danger of lowering morale I ask, is there any hon. member in this house who on second thought will suggest that the officer who has had the most experience of any officer in Canada, the man who has been awarded more decorations for valour than any other officer in Canada, the man who at his own expense has given such unlimited time to the advancement of the reserve forces, army, navy and air, is in fact criticizing the members of any of those forces when he makes such statements in this house as he did in this debate? What I have just said applies in various degrees to others who have spoken on this subject, whose record on the field of battle in the last war precludes any suggestion that they
Committee on Defence Expenditure would in any way seek to attack our armed forces, or to minimize their effectiveness, or in any way interfere with their morale.
No, Mr. Speaker; the one danger to morale that lies in this report, or in the Auditor General's report, or in any of the other disclosures would be the knowledge in the minds of those now in uniform that nothing effective was going to be done to deal with these irregularities which have occurred.
Every day that elapses without that kind of action which indicates an acceptance of the kind of responsibility that should be shown does raise questions which could interfere with morale; and it is with that thought in mind that I and others in this house have urged that the government act without delay on the report now before it, and that they also conduct a wider complete inquiry into the whole organization and administration of the armed services.
I have already suggested, and I repeat the suggestion, that if the government really meant what it said when it expressed its confidence in Mr. Currie, that it seek to have Mr. Currie conduct that wider inquiry with the same independence and impartiality that he showed in conducting the inquiry of which we now have a report. Mr. Currie of course would be free to do that if this diversionary action, to use a term that we have heard, were not employed, and the device were not adopted of having an inquiry into a report of another inquirer.
Let us see what would happen even if for the first time we did receive the kind of report from this committee that we had hoped we might receive when we urged the setting up of such a committee. That report would come back to this house. It would have no effect except as a finding of fact, corresponding with Mr. Currie's finding of fact, until it had been brought to the attention of this house by a motion for its approval. Are we to have another inquiry into an inquiry into an inquiry? That is what this procedure suggests. No, Mr. Speaker; right at this moment young men in uniform are facing a dangerous and terrible enemy on the field of battle. Young men in the Royal Canadian Air Force in France and in Britain at this very time are manning the aircraft of the squadrons which are over there as part of the joint defence of our freedom.
In Germany young Canadians in the army are carrying the name of Canada on their shoulders in a manner which gives us justification for pride in the Canadian uniform wherever it may be. At sea and in many parts of the world young men and women are offering the highest form of service to their country, to their fellow Canadians, that

There are also the Canadian taxpayers, burdened down with the weight of the taxes they are now shouldering as part of their responsibilities as citizens of this country. When we have urged over and over again that steps be taken to reduce taxes and increase the efficiency of the administration of the departments, particularly of the Department of National Defence, we have been told that no savings could be made because nearly all the expenditure was for fixed obligations such as social services and for national defence. We have been left with the impression that the government thinks that national defence expenditure is sacrosanct. Any suggestion that there might be improvement in the methods adopted has been met by the improper suggestion on some occasions that we were urging that we reduce the defence forces of this country. No matter what other results there may be from the Currie report, there is this definite result. No person who has read the findings in that report can hope to have his statement taken seriously if he now contends that there is no waste, extravagance, or improper use of public funds. And even without the Currie report, the Auditor General's report makes it perfectly clear that there are things that :an be done to bring about a more effective supervision of public spending in this country.
There have been strong statements on both sides. When the statement of the government was made, along with the introduction of the report on the 15th of December, immediately she suggestion was made that any criticism was to be taken by the government as being political criticism. When the carefully considered statement of the government was made two days later, on the evening of December 17, there in a fully prepared state-nent on behalf of the government we had he same implication conveyed to us and to ;he people of Canada. That was not welcomed >y members of the opposition. Similar suggestions have not been welcomed since that ;ime because they are wholly out of keeping with the responsibility of every member in he House of Commons. The government has lot welcomed criticism from this side of the louse. That is its right. It has given very rigorous and very noticeable evidence of its ibjection to some of the comments which lave been made.
Let us accept that as part of the debate >n a report which, doubtless, came as a surmise to every member in the house except


those who had the special privilege of an earlier consideration of it. But let us accept the fact that, no matter what debate there has been, and no matter whether there has been objection on one side or on the other to things that have been said, we are dealing with the security of Canada, with the way in which young men and women will be permitted to defend this country in the uniforms they wear so proudly, and also with the assurance that the money paid out by our heavily-burdened taxpayers is being used in the best possible way for the defence of our native land.
These are the issues that are really before us. And it is in that light I hoped that at this time the government would reconsider its position, would depart from its rigid stand of defending the indefensible, and would depart from its diversionary activities in regard to the real core of the issue before us. I think I can safely speak on behalf of all members in the opposition in this instance, although without previous consultation with them, when I say I feel sure that hon. members in all parts of the house would applaud a decision by the government, if we received evidence of its determination to act effectively at this time.
We have before us a subamendment, which will be the first question upon which hon. members will be called upon to vote. Members of this party could have presented a subaimendment in that form, but we did not do so because we hoped it would be possible to deal with the need for a wider inquiry, and at the same time do that without being called upon to accept, even in form, the proposition that the Currie report should be submitted to a further inquiry. However, as a result of the procedure adopted by the government we were denied that opportunity. And while I regret that it has become necessary for a subamendment to embrace, in form at any rate, the amendment of the government, I welcome the fact that, subsequent to the subamendment which we put forward and which was ruled out of order, another has been introduced which will call for a straight vote on the question of whether this inquiry is to be carried into the wider field of all the rest of the department, which has not been covered by the Currie report.
For that reason I am sure the subamendment will receive general support among members of the opposition. However, we are still in a position where something else might happen. In all earnestness I do urge the government between now and eight o'clock, when the debate will be resumed, to follow a course which will not impose upon

its own members any question of a vote of confidence, or any reflection by those who normally support that government on what it has done.
I urge the government, in all earnestness, and having due regard to the full significance of the disclosures made in this report, to state to the house that it will act upon the Currie report; that the defence expenditure committee will be free to carry out the work for which it was set up, and to deal with other subjects; and that there will be a full inquiry into all the rest of the defence services by Mr. Currie or someone equally competent to carry forward an inquiry of this nature.
That would bring us back to the position we were in last April, when the government indicated its desire to get at the facts and deal with them. May I anticipate only one answer to this suggestion. We have been told that already the government has taken action to deal with so many of these things that, for all practical purposes, the job has been done. Mr. Speaker, if that were so there would be no need for the Currie report to go before this committee. If the government really believes that everything has been done that should be done under this report, then the only purpose in referring the Currie report to that committee is to try to cast reflections upon the accuracy of the report.
I hope that is not their purpose, because that would stultify the effectiveness of the committee and would drag out proceedings which, at this important time, could be directed to very important subjects which would come properly before the committee. I refer again to the statement by Mr. Currie that the chaotic conditions of the accounting methods are such that no one knows what the losses really were, and represent those of only one camp, amounting in value to perhaps 3 per cent of the total value of all the property of the Department of National Defence. The report does demonstrate the need for a wider and similarly complete inquiry. I hope we will have it.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 18. to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952, with respect to the quorum of the House of Commons.
House of Commons Quorum
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is one which concerns us, and I hope it will be considered by members of this House of Commons as a matter which should receive our serious and earnest attention. The proposal contained in the bill is that we make a slight increase in the quorum required for the transaction of business in the House of Commons. As hon. members know, at the present time the quorum is 20 members, as set out in section 48 of the British North America Act, which reads:
The presence of at least twenty members of the House of Commons shall be necessary to constitute a meeting of the house for the exercise of its powers; and for that purpose the Speaker shall be reckoned as a member.
As has been indicated in the explanatory notes to the printed copy of the bill, this figure of 20 members was decided upon back in 1867 when the membership of the House of Commons was set at 181. For my part I think that that was a very small quorum to propose for a house of 181 members. Nevertheless, in suggesting that the quorum should be increased I have felt that it might be difficult to persuade some hon. members that we go beyond the proportion that was fixed at that time.
The figure of 30 members as a quorum which my bill suggests was arrived at by the process of simple arithmetic. As hon. members know, the membership in this House of Commons is now 262. By reason of the amendment to the British North America Act passed last year respecting representation in the House of Commons, and the Representation Act of 1952, the terms of which were based on the amendment to the constitution to which I have just referred, we will have 265 members in the House of Commons that will meet following the forthcoming election. If 20 members were considered to be a quorum when the membership of the house was 181, simple arithmetic makes it clear that in the light of our larger membership the quorum would be 29 and a fraction. I have suggested the nearest round figure of 30. All that this bill proposes is that we change the quorum for the transaction of business in the House of Commons from 20 to 30 members.
This is the first occasion on which this bill has come before the house for consideration, but it is not the first occasion on which it has been on the order paper. As a result of it having been on the order paper on previous occasions, I have had comments made to me about it and I have noted comments in the press. The only serious criticism that has been made, a criticism which I readily accept, is that the figure of 30 seems too low.

House of Commons Quorum
The so-called man on "the street, to whom we often refer, is really shocked when he learns that our present quorum is only 20. At times I have asked unsuspecting people who do not know our rules what they supposed was the quorum in the House of Commons. Many times the answer has been, "I suppose a bare majority." Others have suggested 100, and the lowest figure I have ever had suggested to me by an unsuspecting person was the figure of 50. Yet here we are with a quorum of only 20.
Some of those who have commented on my bill are amazed that I have not proposed an even larger figure than 30. I want to make it clear that for my part I would like to see a much larger quorum. I think it only proper that for the transaction of this nation's business there should be required to be in attendance a much larger proportion of the membership of this House of Commons.
However, knowing the tendency that exists to be guided by precedent and tradition, for the purposes of this bill I am prepared to go along with the proportion established by the fathers of confederation. It is in that spirit that I have arrived at the figure of 30. I earnestly hope that the house will consider favourably this bill and will support the view that our responsibilities are such that there should be a few more of us here for the transaction of business than the minimum figure of 20.
Not only have I discussed this matter with people outside the house; not only have I noticed comments in the press on it. There have been some comments on this matter made to me by other members of the house. The difficulty raised by some who have spoken to me is whether or not it would always be possible to get as many as 30 members in the house, particularly at a time when committees were meeting. No one can deny the fact that when several important committees are meeting it might seem to be difficult to get a quorum in all the committees and also have an adequate attendance in the house at the same time. I admit that that seems to be difficult, but I submit most seriously that it should not be.
As hon. members know, the facilities in this building in the way of rooms available for the holding of committee meetings are much more limited than one would think when he looks at the amazing size of this building itself. Hon members know that we cannot hold more than four or five committee meetings at one and the same time. Committees vary in size, but even if we take the outside figure as an average of the normal committee meeting and assume that we have five committees going on at the same time

with 30 members in each committee, that makes only a total of 150 members, leaving 112 members available for attendance in the House of Commons.

No, I did not give those figures. As a matter of fact, I am a little surprised that this matter came up today and I may say frankly that I have not looked them up. I am basing my whole argument on what would seem to be reasonable and responsible on our own part. I agree with the hon. member that the other figures would be interesting, and perhaps they can be ascertained and brought to bear upon the question. But whatever those figures are, even if they are smaller in proportion, I submit that we owe it to the country we serve by the duties that we perform here to require of ourselves a higher rate of attendance in the house than is required by section 48 of the British North America Act as it now stands. I repeat what I started out by saying, namely, that my bill does not ask for these much higher quorum figures to which I have referred. My bill asks for only 30, which is simply maintaining the proportion established by the fathers of confederation in 1867.

There are other aspects of the whole question of attendance that might be gone into. I have been known to take cracks, shall I say, at a certain institution that meets at the other end of this building; but so far as the question of attendance is concerned may I say that I note with interest and approval that in the other place a daily record is kept of the attendance of Their Honours, the members of the Senate. We have no such record here. There are times when we would not need a record. During the last week or so the interest in the subject that has been under discussion has been such that we have had excellent attendance in the house and in the galleries as well. But it is our responsibility to give serious and responsible attention to the business of the country whether or not it is a matter of great, dramatic and spectacular interest.
For that reason I press upon the house the serious consideration of this matter. I ask hon. members to face the fact that the change suggested in the bill is ever so slight. As a matter of fact it can be argued that it does not introduce any change at all. It merely says that we agree to maintain as a quorum the same proportion of our total membership that was agreed upon by the fathers of confederation in 1867. Despite the fact that I am not a lawyer-and one can always be corrected on these interpretations-I would point out that the wording of section 48 in the original British North America Act does not, in my view, say that the quorum can be no higher than 20. It merely says that there must be at least 20 members, and I have often taken the view that it would have been within the right of parliament, even before we had the right to amend the British North America Act, to fix a higher figure. In other words I am wondering if the fathers of confederation expected that 20 would remain as the figure. I wonder if they did not leave it to the House of Commons itself to make that figure a little higher if the house wished to do so. At any rate, we have not done so in all the years from 1867 until the present. Despite the increases that have taken place in the membership, the quorum has remained at that same terribly low figure of 20 members. Now that the matter has been put before the house in a formal way I hope we will correct the situation.
There is one other aspect about the bill which I might take the liberty of calling to the attention of the house, merely because I am sure it is of interest to many hon. members. This bill, like the one last year that changed the rules regarding redistribution, involves an amendment to the British North
House of Commons Quorum America Act. The bill with respect to redistribution, which was piloted through the house last year in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), I believe, was the first bill to amend the British North America Act, the constitution of this country, on the basis of legislation passed by this parliament and by this parliament alone. The bill now before us might be referred to as the first private member's bill amending the British North America Act since we obtained for ourselves in 1949 the right to amend that act in Canada in respect of matters exclusively federal.
This bill is drawn in exactly the same form as the bill introduced last year by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, at least in so far as its being a bill that amends the British North America Act is concerned. For my part I have been interested in this question, and have had the opportunity of discussing it with a number of authorities in the constitutional field. One question that used to concern me about this whole matter was a purely technical one. How was it possible for us in the parliament of Canada, even after the amendment of the British North America Act was passed which gave us the right to amend our own constitution, to amend what in effect seemed to be a statute of another country, namely the British North America Act passed originally in the parliament of the United Kingdom in 1867?
The opinion that was expressed to us on that point last year in the redistribution committee is, I think, perhaps novel but also interesting and rather conclusive. It was that the British North America Act of 1867 was, in purely legal and technical terms, an enactment of the crown which was passed with the advice and consent of the parliament of the United Kingdom. All we are doing when we amend that act in Canada is arranging for the crown to amend the same act which the crown originally enacted, the only difference being that in the meantime there has been a change as to who advises the crown with respect to this act, and in this instance it would be the parliament of Canada advising the crown rather than the parliament of the United Kingdom.
I think it is fair to say that, until the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration brought in his bill last year respecting redistribution, there were different patterns that might have been followed in amending our own constitution by decision of this parliament, and that any one of two or three different patterns might have been justified. I think it is also fair to say that, once a pattern has been established, there being plenty of lawyers around
1166	HOUSE OF
House of Commons Quorum this place, the tendency will be to say that that is the correct pattern and that is the pattern to follow henceforth.
In any case the bill follows that pattern so far as its technique is concerned. It is a bill of the parliament of Canada amending what is known as our constitution, the British North America Act. We have the right to advise the crown to enact legislation in this form by virtue of the amendment to the British North America Act of 1949 which gave the parliament of Canada the power to amend its own constitution with respect to matters that are exclusively federal. The issue in the bill is obviously a matter exclusively federal. It is even narrower than that; it is a matter that concerns us right here in the House of Commons. Therefore I think there can be no doubt as to our right to deal with the subject matter of the bill.
I also feel, as I have already said, that there is surely no doubt as to the simplicity of the request, as to the fact that it is a very minor change that is being requested. It merely proposes that we maintain the same proportion that was established in 1867.
I hope this will not be looked upon as a bill coming from any one party in the house, but rather as a bill presented to the rest of the members by one member who is interested in these things, and that it will be given very serious consideration in all parts of this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposition the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has put forward, if it stands simply on the basis of carrying forward to the present time the proportion that was established in 1867 which the quorum of the house should bear to the total membership of the house, seems to have much to commend it to reasonable people. However, there is another aspect of the matter which all hon. members must bear in mind.
The proposal just put forward now on behalf of the government by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) I think is one that will meet with general approval in this house. This is a matter that may very well be considered in relation to the other matters that will, I take it, in due course be referred to the committee on rules for consideration. But whether the matter is dealt with conclusively here or whether it is deliberated on by the committee on rules, there will be no escape from one consideration.
When the fathers of confederation agreed upon their proposals for the formation of a nation on this northern half of the continent, they did not leave it to the parliament, nor to the House of Commons, to establish the quorum of the house. This matter was never viewed hitherto as a matter of concern simply to the House of Commons. That is not the way the fathers of confederation drafted the structure of confederation in this respect. They made it a provision of the British North America Act that the quorum should be fixed as set forth in section 48 of the act.
It might impress many hon. members that this is after all a relatively simple matter. You just change one figure, one word in the British North America Act. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is quite true that the amendment that is under discussion now does not do more than that in form. It simply changes the word "twenty" in section 48 of the British North America Act to "thirty". But before we can do that, Mr. Speaker, we must have due regard for some of the implications of the step we are taking.
The views which we of the Progressive Conservative party hold in regard to the subject of amendment of the British North America Act have been set forth on previous occasions, the last of which was the debate on the redistribution bill on June 12, 1952. While the matter before us now looks to be so simple, it nevertheless presents the same problems, Mr. Speaker, as to the right of parliament to proceed to amend the British North America Act without consultation with anyone.

The fact that this problem arises again in a situation where the amendment proposed is in form so simple I think serves to emphasize once more, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the country needs today the legislative adoption of a proper formula for amendment within Canada of the British North America Act. That in turn requires the resumption, at as early a date as possible, of the conference which was called some three years ago-the dominion-provincial conference- with a view to working out by agreement some formula for amending the British North America Act within Canada.
It will be recalled by hon. members that when the provinces were asked to indicate their views on the method by which the act should be amended in various respects, there was quite a variety of answers. In view of the fact that this particular bill has been called unexpectedly today, Mr. Speaker, I have not had an opportunity to review the recommendations made by the provincial governments at that time with reference to the amendment of this particular section of the act. It may well be that many of the provinces at that time indicated they had no objection to parliament taking unto itself the right to amend this section simply by act of parliament. But I am not prepared to assume that with reference to all the provinces, because the views expressed by some of the provinces were quite strong as to the necessity for working out a general formula for amendment on the basis of that formula being satisfactory to all provinces, although the formula itself would make provision for the amendment of various provisions in the British North America Act, under varying terms. In some cases it would be by consent of a majority of the provinces, in other cases by varying proportions, leading up, in the case of some provisions of the British North America Act, to the requirement that the particular provision of the act should not be amended without the consent of all the provinces.
Surely what is required, not simply in relation to this particular matter but in relation to the whole question of the constitutional position of Canada, is that there should be a prompt resumption of that dominion-provincial conference. This particular section 48 is by no means the only section of the British North America Act that is crying aloud today for some legislative consideration. In the British North America Act today, as the fundamental law of Canada, we have provisions that are quite outworn; and the continued existence of those provisions, Mr. Speaker, stresses the necessity for a dominion-provincial conference with a view to changing them.

Mr. Speaker, the point I was making-and I did not intend to elaborate on it at length-was that this bill, as do many other circumstances, points to the necessity for the resumption of that dominion-provincial conference. What I was about to do when you rose, Mr. Speaker, was to recall to the minds of hon. members that in sections like 55, 56 and 57 we have, in this fundamental written law of the constitution today, provisions that are completely outworn and that emphasize the necessity for our trying to bring the constitution up to date by the only method by which, in my submission, it can be brought up to date, namely by working out an amending formula that will be acceptable to the provinces.
This consideration, Mr. Speaker, is one that must be borne in mind, in my submission, even though this bill at a later point in this session may be referred to the house committee on rules. Had the fathers of confederation regarded this matter of the quorum of the house as simply a matter of the internal organization of the house, then this provision contained in section 48 would not have found its way into the act. It would have been left to the house to establish its own quorum. It may be that there are many today who, if this question were approached de novo, would take the position that it should be left to the house. But that is not the position in which we find ourselves.
As a result of the amendment of the British North America Act that was adopted in 1949 -an unwise form of amendment of the British North America Act, in my submission, in the ill-considered formula that it contained for carrying out amendments of the British North America Act-the position in which we find ourselves at the moment simply means this. Because this provision is in the British North America Act and the government says that it is a federal matter, then this result follows: if it is in the act, you simply proceed


by a bill, give it three readings, and change it just as you wish. If it were a rule of the house, presumably the house would simply change it by resolution providing for an amendment of the rules of the house. That is the only difference left. We in this part of the house do not think that the constitution of this country, the fundamental written law of Canada, should be equated simply with a rule of this house.
No matter how simple this matter may be in form, it has implications of great importance. Because of the fact that the federal government has not made any move to call for a resumption of the dominion-provincial conference, one province-Quebec-has recently found it necessary to propose the appointment of a royal commission to review the whole question of federal-provincial relations. In the face of situations like that, surely the need for the resumption of that dominion-provincial conference on the British North America Act and methods of amending it is imperative today.

With great respect, Mr. Speaker, may I say you have stated that this may involve the amendment of the rules of the house. The very point I am seeking to argue at the moment is that what is involved in this bill is an amendment of the British North America Act. The legislative position created by an unwise amendment of the British North America Act by the parliament at Westminster in 1949, at the instance of this parliament, makes this provision of the British North America Act mean little more than just a rule of the house. It can be changed in practically the same way that we can amend any rule of the house. It seems to me that is one of the implications of this present bill that ought to be laid before this house and ought to be considered by this house with the utmost seriousness.
As to the form of the amendment, I wish to make it clear that I am expressing no objection in principle to an increase in the quorum of the house. Just on the basis of mathematics alone I think there may be a good deal to be said-as was stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in introducing this bill-for

increasing the quorum so that the fraction it represents of the total membership today may bear a reasonable relation to the fraction that was established in 1867. But the way to deal with this matter is not, in my submission, to treat it simply as a matter in which parliament has a perfectly free hand to proceed without consultation. There are implications here that go much farther and they are implications which, in my submission, are not going to be disposed of merely by referring the matter to the rules committee. I would not oppose that course for consideration of the matter but, Mr. Speaker, that will not end the problems that are presented by this bill. There will still be the fundamental problem that here you are dealing with a provision in the fundamental written constitution of this country.
What is so badly needed today is to avoid a piecemeal approach to this question. What is needed is not an approach that is going to make it more difficult to have that form of constitutional amendment which is required but which will instead make provision for a formula for dealing with all amendments that may be sought by the Canadian people. What is required here is due acknowledgment of the fact that the British North America Act is a fundamental constitutional document, and that in making changes in that fundamental constitutional document more should be required than simply a decision from time to time in this house or in the other place.
I urge, Mr. Speaker, that the only way out of the problem that has been created by an unwise amendment of the British North America Act in 1949 is the one I have proposed, namely that this and other matters requiring consideration in reference to needed amendments of the British North America Act should be the subject matter of consideration in an immediate resumption of the dominion-provincial conference on amendment of the British North America Act.

When I adjourned the debate last Tuesday I was examining certain views that had been expressed in a previous debate by some of the main supporters of the amendment which is now before the house. I had occasion more particularly to refer to the debate on the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act of 1950, and to the remarks of both the leader of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I also referred to statements made by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), and at the time of the adjournment I still had one or two statements by the hon. member for Spadina that I wished to put on the record.
All those quotations which I have offered for the consideration of the house were intended at that time-and I use them in this debate for the same purpose-to indicate how important it is for the welfare of the Canadian worker and for the peaceful development of our industry as a whole that the utmost freedom should be left to collective bargaining between the two partners in industry.
During the debate on the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act of two years ago, the

Industrial Relations
hon. member for Spadina placed a great deal of importance on this basic principle of free collective bargaining in industry. I have quoted a few sentences from his remarks in this regard, and X wish to add this one which will be found on page 41 of Hansard for the fall session of 1950:
I believe that compulsory arbitration means the death of collective bargaining. It is all very well to say that we shall apply this principle only in this case, but we have done damage to a fundamental principle of freedom.
In my several participations in debates on this matter of the voluntary revocable checkoff, I have always sustained that particular point. Should this bill be passed and the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act be amended to make it compulsory to have the voluntary revocable check-off, we would, using the words of the hon. member for Spadina, be doing damage to a fundamental principle of freedom.
I should like to quote from the speech that the mover of this amendment made in the same debate in the fall of 1950, and which I submit is most relevant to the point. It will be found at page 41 of Hansard of that session:
I share the view that has just been expressed by the hon. member for Spadina, and which was also put forward .by my leader and by the member for Vancouver East, that it is in the public interest also, indeed that it is of primary importance, that there be no interference with the principle of free collective bargaining.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) also participated in that debate and expounded his views on the basic principle of industrial relations in this country and on free collective bargaining. He had this to say, as reported at page 48 of Hansard:
I am convinced that you cannot write a trade-union agreement on the floor of the House of Commons. The former minister of labour made that statement many times and I agreed; you cannot do it.
We are setting a precedent that will be taken as a pattern by industry in this country if and when the bargaining gets a little tough. The simple and easy thing to do then will be to break off, throw the matter into the lap of the government and have a bill passed.
On page 49 the hon. member had this to say:
I believe we did a good job of writing a national labour code, but do not forget that this bill automatically wipes out many provisions of that code as it applies to this dispute.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) also participated in the debate, and made an interesting contribution which I should like to place on record, when he said:
I object as strenuously as does any other member of this house to compulsion of any sort in labour-management disputes or in anything that has to do with collective bargaining.
IMr. Cote (Verdun-La Salle).]
While I cannot recall definitely the stand taken by the hon. member for York West on measures of this kind when they were presented to the house in years past, I wish to stress that all the other hon. members to whom I have referred have approved the principle of this amending bill, and by so doing have taken a position which is in direct conflict with the statements made by them during the debate on the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act in 1950.
If on the one hand parliament should preserve by all possible means the freedom of action of both management and labour when they get together and attempt in good faith to reach common agreement, then the amending bill proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) becomes- quite objectionable. It may not mean very much in itself, because what it proposes to introduce is, after all, only the slightest possible measure of union security, described in the amending bill as the voluntary revocable check-off. But once the principle is applied of interference by parliament in matters which have thus far been left with labour and management to discuss, and upon which they can surely agree, there will be no limit to the powers of parliament in future years for further interference, in circumstances which might be much more important than those surrounding the voluntary revocable check-off.
While I have not the exact reference before me, I do recollect that on one occasion in the past, when the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was discussing a similar bill, I asked him if the bill were passed whether he and his party would be satisfied to leave it at that, and give a guarantee that it would not be considered as a precedent; that they would not come here year after year asking for more and more interference by parliament in matters of collective bargaining. He said, "No, that is not the end; that is just the beginning". I can vouch for his reply on that occasion-. So, that means a policy of opening the door wider and wider as the years go by, and some day bringing parliament to a position of dictating by statute what the wages, hours of work and conditions of work will be in any plant or industry coming under the jurisdiction of parliament.

Now, if it was not a stolen document, what was it?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre replied:
Well, it was a document that had come into our possession. We did not know the ultimate source of it, but we were ready to believe that the person who sent it to us was concerned over the fact that changes were being made and he seemed most anxious that the matter might be raised in public.
You will all recall that the only report, the signed report, was tabled on December 15. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) wrote me a letter on January 17 reporting on the investigation by the police which showed that a copy of the draft stolen from the print shop had been stolen between November 25 and November 29. How did the

Committee on Defence Expenditure person who had stolen the report between November 25 and November 29 know there were changes in the report as tabled on December 15?
Then according to a statement by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, reported in the Montreal Gazette of this morning, the draft came into the possession of his leader only-and I quote-"a few days before December 15". How did the person who delivered the stolen copy, if he was different, as the hon. member has said, from the person who took it-how he would know that precisely, I do not know-how would the person who delivered the stolen copy of the draft to the C.C.F. know that changes were being made when that could only be ascertained by a comparison of the two copies on December 15?
