The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, "The government intends to do nothing". There were other hon. members who spoke to the same effect. I do not want to repeat, and I am sure nobody wants me to repeat, what I said a week ago; but I did tell the house precisely what the government and the department had done and were doing in consequence of the report, which I referred to as a very important document, and I referred to its constructive recommendations. Then I went on to deal with the recommendations under different classes. I referred to those which were being implemented before we ever received Mr. Currie's report at all, those which were being considered, and at the end of my remarks I referred to two which we considered so far as not being desirable in the circumstances.
That is not taking the report lightly. I have dealt with the report as it deserves to be dealt with. I have recounted to the house the approach we made to it, the consideration we gave to it and what we have done in consequence of it. I also said it would continue to receive consideration. I thought there were a number of matters raised in the
Committee on Defence Expenditure report, particularly the recommendations in parts II, III and IV, concerning which it would be very useful indeed to have the views of the committee and also those of Mr. Currie. If this matter had not become the political issue that it has been made, I can tell the house that I would have been in continuous consultation with Mr. Currie since he made his report working out with him ways and means whereby we might implement it as expeditiously as possible in exactly the same way as we in the department were in consultation with him and his representatives throughout the whole period of his investigation, which was carried on as a joint operation.
It was in that spirit that the job was approached and it is in that spirit that it would have been carried through. But I hope the defence expenditure committee will be able to look into the report, have the officials of the department there and see whether the views I have already expressed on the cost of implementing some of the recommendations of the report are correct or whether the estimates of cost are as low as they can be made. Perhaps we can find ways and means of building fences and providing security guards at lower costs than those I gave the house last Tuesday, but these costs are the lowest at which we have been able to arrive so far. Some of them throw grave doubt upon the desirability of some of the additional security measures to which reference has been made.

I think I had better finish.
Another thing, Mr. Speaker, at which the hon. members opposite have been pounding away, is that I gave the opposition and the country the assurance that everything was perfect. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) at page 1069 of Hansard said:
... he gave us the assurance that everything was perfect . . .
Similar expressions have been uttered by virtually every speaker for the Conservative opposition. Now, I have a pretty good filing system and index, and I have searched the records since I became Minister of National Defence in 1946 for any single occasion on which I said that everything was perfect, or anything to that effect. It is another myth the opposition are seeking to build up in order that when they find, as I know, that everything is not perfect they will say "but he said it was perfect".
Today the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) quoted three passages
1174

Committee on Defence Expenditure from speeches of mine in the house in 1948, 1950 and 1951. The quotations were, I think, intended to support the assertion that I said everything was perfect. Well, I ask hon. members to read Hansard for this afternoon to see whether they can extract any such assertion from those three statements, even widely spaced, and putting them together out of their context. Indeed, I will find a dozen statements in which I brought before the house the difficulties and problems of building up defence forces during this period after the second world war. I assure hon. members that I was fully conscious of those difficulties and, sometimes, conscious of the fact that not very much in the way of support was given in that very difficult task.
Now, sir, reference was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to the report of the Auditor General. That is a report made to parliament. In it the Auditor General makes his observations of the activities of various departments and agencies of government. The report has a total of 43 pages. It has 107 numbered paragraphs. Twelve of those paragraphs are devoted to national defence.
One section to which the Leader of the Opposition referred appears at page 24 of the report of the Auditor General. It deals with the methods of keeping accounts for stores. Here I would suggest that the Leader of the Opposition, in his remarks this afternoon, appeared as it were to put into the mouth of the Auditor General, in presenting his report, more than I think you will find in the report itself. Hansard and the report will of course speak for themselves. In paragraph 56 the report refers to service forces accounting:
Stores. Surveys made oi accounting systems-* there are at least eight-indicate that no sustained effort has been made to achieve uniformity in systems within the services. The result is that mandatory directives are specialized, particularly with respect to the army. Various other special problems also exist, in particular:
Now, sir, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to our uttering a blast upon receipt of the report of the Auditor General. There was no blast. The Canadian Press, the British United Press, and other sections of the press asked for comments on the background of the Auditor General's report and a statement was issued which gives some of the background. I will read from part of it.
The storekeeping systems in use by the services were explained at some length to the defence expenditures committee last year. While they vary in detail, the basic principles underlying the systems are the same in all three services, and within each service. The organization for administering
[Mr. Claxton.l

them differs among the services by reason of the differences in organization in each service to provide for the essentially different tasks of each. In the army, the ordnance corps, the army service corps, the medical corps, the dental corps and the engineer corps each have their own stores and accounting organizations. In this respect the Canadian army is similar to the British and United States armies with which they work. These systems of each corps differ in varying degrees to meet the specialized needs of the corps they serve. Continuous efforts are made to improve these systems and while uniformity is not an objective for its own sake where an improvement in one system could be usefully applied in the others, it is.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there are further notes. I suggest to the house that this is a matter which can properly go before the defence expenditure committee and be considered by it as was done last year.
The Leader of the Opposition, and also the member for Winnipeg North Centre, referred to the case of a brigadier who had received from the army both a retirement allowance and pay as a civilian employee in respect of the same period. That is dealt with at page 26 of the report, in paragraph 65. Here the Auditor General makes an observation drawing, as he properly should, the attention of parliament to this fact.
This grows out of the application by the Department of National Defence of the provisions of the law and regulations relating to retirement. Under these laws and regulations an officer or man on completion of a certain number of years of service is entitled -just like a civil servant-to a number of months of leave with pay upon retirement. In this case, and in numerous cases in this and other government departments, officers and men entitled to retirement leave have wished to join the civil service. Indeed, in our case, this officer was very much sought after and we wanted him to come to work at once. In accordance with the authority given to us by the treasury board, the civilian end of the department paid him his salary as a civilian worker while he got his retirement allowance for the period of leave which he was not getting. That was strictly in accordance with a ruling of the treasury board dated February 4, 1944.
The Auditor General feels that this should be drawn to the attention of members. It is another matter which I suggest could go before the committee on defence expenditure. Last year, when the observations of the Auditor General were before that committee, the committee examined them, heard the observations of the department, and appeared to be completely satisfied therewith. I hope the same result will obtain this year.
Now, sir, in the course of the discussion a number of points were made to which I

have only a brief moment to refer. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) was good enough in his1 very courteous remarks to extend to me a welcome back, which I appreciated. Both he and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) referred to the reduction in size of the forces, and demobilization at the end of the second world war, having brought about or contributed to the situation in which the army works services found themselves at the time of Korea. I do not believe that can be successfully argued. There was no time at the end of the second world war when we were not engaged in building up the permanent peacetime array. Officers and men were taken on at the rate at which they were available, and at which spaces and money were available. The build-up was steady. Had we kept on forces in being and had we postponed demobilization, the disposal of surplus war stores and the conversion to peacetime use of the productive capacity in factories, I can hear the cry that would have gone up at our delay in getting the boys home and getting the people back to work. As it was, the speed with which the operation was carried out was a major factor in establishing Canada on a sound economic foundation and the early start in the post-war period contributed greatly to the prosperity which we have enjoyed ever since.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the Prime Minister whether there was not another order issued by the chief of the general staff with regard to the discussion of the Currie report by employees of the department, and the Prime Minister said there was none. The Prime Minister was quite correct. The only order issued by the chief of the general staff was the one read by the Prime Minister. However, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had a unit order which had been issued to a minor unit by the commanding officer, and it was couched in those terms because he had a number of civilians working alongside service personnel. The fact that this had been done was discovered within a matter of days and a correction was entered.
Then the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) asked a number of questions with regard to aircraft, particularly what we were doing to plan and equip ourselves with supersonic aircraft of types more advanced than the F-86 Sabre and the CF-100, which he said were good aeroplanes. Then he went on to say, as reported at page 1077 of Hansard:
-they would be practically useless as effective barriers to such bombers.

I believe that to be a rather modest estimate. I hope it is.

All right; a minimum of five years. I should think that was a fairly sound position. The F-86E is the most advanced type of aircraft in production anywhere. That fact is brought out by the fact that it is being produced by us for Britain to help fill the gap there. It is being used by us in Britain and in France as part of the front line defences of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and it has proved itself in the battlefield in Korea. Not only have the United States-built Sabres proved themselves there, but the Canadian-built Sabres have also done so and, if I may say so, so have the officers of the R.C.A.F.
Then the question is asked: What are we doing to design and to construct a fighter plane with the characteristics necessary for successful combat? There is no fighter having better characteristics for successful combat belonging to us or to our allies today than the F-86E, and when equipped with the more powerful Orenda engines it is believed that it will have characteristics which will enable it to have a considerable life of usefulness against any enemy that might confront us.	However, we are doing preliminary
design work and are working out the characteristics for further long-time development of the CF-100. We work in close co-operation with our allies, the United Kingdom and the United States, with whom we have the closest liaison.
Then the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) referred to the Alaska highway, particularly in 1942 and 1943. I should point out that, as	hon. members know, the
highway and all its operations were only taken over by the Canadian army on April 1, 1946.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the question of security. I should refer again to what I said on this subject a week ago, as reported at page 942 of Hansard, when I recalled that at Petawawa alone the cost of fences necessary to provide security was estimated at $286,000 and the annual cost of the additional guards would be $119,000. At Camp Borden the figures were respectively $346,000 and $139,000. In connection with these questions you find that you must

Committee on Defence Expenditure strike a balance between how much you gain through reducing your potential losses by investing in capital equipment and putting on additional personnel.
As I pointed out the other day and as was pointed out by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), in his constructive and fair speech, the most striking example of that feature was at Farnham where, in order to save a possible loss of property having a value of probably $10,000, it would have been necessary to spend between $25,000 and $30,000 a year on guards.
The question has been asked: Why should we refer the Currie report to a committee? In the speech I made the other night and in my remarks tonight I have indicated some of the reasons why that should be done. I can also point to others. Other matters which are particularly interesting, and upon which it would be most helpful and constructive to have the views of the committee would be the simplification of the procedure for establishing positions and the machinery for filling positions. As the Currie report states and as I stated-and as everyone knows- the main reason for the situation which gave rise to the opportunities that occurred at Petawawa was a shortage of staff. As I said the other day, we have full documentation on each of the recommendations, and will be prepared to put before the committee in detail the efforts made to secure adequate establishments and staffs, both within the department and through the civil service commission. Having regard to the circumstances; the fact that this new system had only begun to be introduced and that its introduction was only likely to be completed in 1951; the fact that Korea intervened in June, 1950; the fact that since then we have had the great build-up in the operations and size of the armed forces, I think the committee, in the end, will be satisfied that even with all the advantage of hindsight it is difficult to see today what should have been done-and nobody here has suggested it-to prevent what happened. We must use every possible endeavour to see that everything reasonably economic to promote the efficient operation of the department and proper accounting is carried through. But once again, Mr. Speaker, I would remind hon. members that in this matter there was no failure in operations. There was a breakdown, as Mr. Currie calls it, although I think it was not so much a breakdown as the fact that the new system never had a chance to be established. It was this which produced a lack of more adequate accounts in the most difficult type of stores, the accounts for these engineering and building stores at a
(Mr. Claxton.]
place in which, like other establishments across Canada, there was a great amount of construction going on.
Now, sir, at the beginning of his speech the Leader of the Opposition made reference to an amendment which the opposition had proposed to make. Of course it is appreciated that that amendment was not before the house. He suggested that the government had employed a device, though he said it was a perfectly proper device, to exclude its consideration. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did on that occasion was something that I really cannot imagine the Leader of the Opposition, or for that matter many leaders of parties, doing, namely forgoing his right to speak in order that on my return from abroad, I might take advantage of the first opportunity to deal with a matter which had come up during my absence. I am sure that had that not been done it would have been a subject of criticism.

-that Mr. Currie be asked to conduct a further inquiry into the many other expenditures and commitments covered by the terms of the resolution. Without doubt the minister is responsible for the administration of his department, and quite openly has expressed no desire to escape the responsibility. I am of the opinion that the greater responsibility is not on the minister but on the government as a whole. To expect one minister to administer a department of such gigantic size as the Department of National Defence, having supervision over the expenditure of over $2,000 million, is to invite
Committee on Defence Expenditure the very things to happen that are indicated in the Currie report.
There is no doubt about it that rather late realization of this fact has caused the government to consider and advance proposals for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence. Personally I think that is all to the good. But I am quite sure everyone will recognize that under present conditions the minister has an intolerable amount of office work. I understand that the signing of letters even, and the signing of orders is a tremendous physical task alone, and it is far too much for this government to expect such a huge department to be administered by one minister.
I am not capable of making suggestions as to what is best so far as the division of this department is concerned, but I will say this. I have heard a good number of people across this country say they are of the opinion that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) should be brought back and given charge of air, and that possibly we should have an associate minister for the army and an associate minister for the navy. I just offer that suggestion as one that has been given to me by a number of persons who have some experience in military matters, and who are concerned about the present situation and with relieving the minister of a tremendous load.
This evening I really have one main subject to deal with, but before going on with that I want to say that I was very interested to listen to the explanation given to the house this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in connection with the inadvertent mention by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in his radio broadcast of the Prime Minister as receiving certain documents. Knowing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as I do, I know he certainly would not make an intentional misstatement. He did that quite unintentionally. The point is this, that everything that was being done at that time was under the direction of the then minister of justice, the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and with his knowledge. As a matter of fact his personality affected all the events of that day. The government itself used certain documents and certain reports that were acknowledged to be stolen, in the interests of the state and for the safety of the state. No one criticized him on that account at that time.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) I thought dealt very well with the, shall I say, "circumstances alter cases" part of the situation, when he was referring to the government's action so far as
1178	HOUSE OF
Committee on Defence Expenditure the Currie report is concerned when compared with its action on other reports. I quite support what he had to say with respect to the royal commission's report on the Saskatchewan water development, where it is obvious that the gist of the report was in the hands of some of the press some days ago, and members of the House of Commons and people generally throughout Canada were able to read details in various important magazines. Yet we have not heard of any suggestion by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that a search is going to be made to see who leaked that report, or anything of the sort. We feel that circumstances do alter cases, and that possibly there is not quite the same incentive on the part of the government to find out who leaked that report, who stole that report, which has a bearing on government action, as there has seemed to be in connection with the first or working draft of the Currie report.
Before leaving that subject I should like to bring to the attention of the house this fact, that from a reading of the royal commission's report on the Canadian Pacific scandal of 1873, of the records of the house at that time, and of certain correspondence, X think it is quite correct to say that the first Liberal government that ever came into power in Canada after confederation obtained office as the result of a stolen telegram for which a supporter of the Liberal party paid $5,000.
I think that is quite right. It is obvious that the tradition was established at a very early date.
I have said that the great majority of the people are concerned, in the first instance, with the expenditure of their hard-earned tax dollars for defence purposes. I think the people of Canada are willing to pay for a satisfactory and efficient defence; but they certainly want to be assured that those hard-earned tax dollars are being spent in a proper way. That is an aspect of the question which has been dealt with extensively by members who have spoken previously, including those of the Progressive Conservative party, as well as members of my own group and the Social Credit group. I am not going to discuss that matter tonight, but I shall deal with another aspect of the subject which I think is causing a good number of thinking Canadians serious concern.
I have had an opportunity to discuss this matter with people in various walks of life, people who see things seriously, and I think it is quite safe to say there are quite a number of people seriously concerned with one aspect of the Currie report connected with the actions of some of the military personnel in high authority. I refer particularly, first of all, to the tabling by the Prime Minister, at
{Mr. Herridge.]

the time he tabled the Currie report, of a letter written by the chief of the general staff. I refer secondly to the message of the chief of the general staff in the latest issue of the Canadian Army Journal. I refer also to certain comments made by people in the Department of National Defence with respect to the Auditor General's report, as it applied to that department.
I deal with this question because I think at a time like this it is wise to bring it to the attention of the house, so that we may refresh our minds as to the exact meaning of a democracy. A great many editorials have been written about the tabling of the letter from the chief of the general staff, and about his message in the Canadian Army Journal. It is obvious that in some quarters there is great concern about this action. This is not the first time in Canada that a government has had to indicate that in a democracy those in high command in the army-the chief of the general staff and others-must accept their policy and their direction from parliament, through the government.
I should like to refer to the celebrated case in 1904 of Lord Dundonald, general officer commanding, who was dismissed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the then prime minister, for not observing the principle that the civil power must at all times rule the military. This episode took place when the then minister of agriculture, Mr. Fisher, in his capacity as acting minister of militia, cancelled the name of an officer from a list of officers of a new regiment of dragoons, which had been recommended to the council by Lord Dundonald. Speaking at a military banquet in Montreal, Lord Dundonald, at that time general officer commanding troops in Canada, denounced the minister's action as a gross instance of political interference. The case was brought up in parliament, occasioning vigorous debate. Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated that the cabinet was not obliged to accept the general's recommendations, and said:
We are not accustomed to being dragooned in this country; Lord Dundonald, with all the respect I have for him, must learn that this is a responsible government.
I should like now to quote briefly extracts from volume 1 of the queen's regulations and orders for the Canadian army. Section 3, which deals with public, civil employment, and political activities, in article 19.36, headed, "Disclosure of information or opinion", states:
No officer or man shall publish, communicate, or otherwise disclose any information or opinion relating to military subjects acquired as a result of his army service to any person who is not entitled to receive such information or opinion.

And article 19.37 headed, "Permission required to publish writing or deliver address" states:
(1)	The provisions of this article shall not apply to a writing, lecture, address or broadcast confined exclusively to members of the Canadian forces.
(2)	No officer or man shall, whether it purports to be fiction or fact, publish any writing or deliver any lecture, address, or broadcast in any way dealing with military subjects unless permission is first obtained to do so.
At this point I am going to ask the minister a question: In view of the queen's regulations, when writing his message to the army did the general officer commanding obtain permission to make what in the opinion of many members in the House of Commons would be considered a reflection upon parliament?
In that connection, before proceeding further I should like to read a few brief extracts from the message to the Canadian army from the chief of general staff. I realize that this has already been placed on record by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should add that this is a well drafted and well written message, and states:
In recent weeks and months the army has been the target of unremitting attacks from many sources. We have been criticized for the indiscipline of Canadian soldiers. We have been criticized for too much discipline. We have been criticized for extravagance and criticized for not providing a whole host of things which cost a very great deal of money. We have been criticized for lack of morale and accused of complacency and arrogance when we have shown or proclaimed a pride in the Canadian army.
And again:
None of this should give cause for any discouragement or depression. The only justification for the existence of the Canadian army is to defend democracy of which free public criticism is an essential element. Some of this criticism has been, and will continue to be, unfairly biased and irresponsible but that will be as clear to the citizens and taxpayers outside the army as to those that serve in it.
And again:
I charge every soldier to apply himself in all those matters where we clearly need improvement but not to be discouraged or depressed by criticisms which are neither founded on truth nor justified in the light of our positive achievements.
My point is this. In view of the fact that criticism of the operations of the army and of the Department of National Defence has been primarily in this House of Commons during the last twelve months, in view of the fact that there has been criticism in the press as a result of the debate in the House of Commons, we in this group think it is quite improper for the chief of the general staff to write a message to the troops of Canada which obviously, in view of what he has written and of what has occurred in this house, where the criticism of the Department of National Defence originated, can be taken
Committee on Defence Expenditure and has been taken by a great number of people to whom I have spoken about the matter as a criticism of parliament. I just want to go on to another aspect of these regulations. Section 3 of regulation 19.37 states:
No officer or man of the active force or of the reserves when he is on continuous army duty, special duty, or camp training, shall, whether it purports to be fiction or fact, publish any writing or deliver any lecture, address, or broadcast in any way dealing with subjects of a controversial nature affecting other departments of the public service or pertaining to public policy unless permission is first obtained to do so.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question in that connection. We all read the comments and quite clear criticism of the Auditor General's report which, according to the press, originated with high officers in the Department of National Defence. I ask the Prime Minister if those officers who made those comments in the Canadian press on the Auditor General's report had received the permission of the minister to do so. We in this group think it is highly improper for any official of the Department of National Defence or any high military officer to criticize or to comment upon the report of another department when it is issued. If that state of affairs were allowed to continue we would have the deputy minister of one department criticizing the deputy minister of another department.
I challenge anyone on the government side to indicate where in British parliamentary history a senior military officer or a senior official of the department having to do with military affairs, the war department as it is called in England, has criticized in public or in the press the report or statement of the official having a capacity equal to that of the Auditor General of Canada. It just is not done. I suggest in the same way that it is quite improper and is not fair to the officials who are being criticized or whose recommendations are being commented upon.
I am not going to delay the house at great length, but I feel keenly about this question because I think it is fundamental. I should like to make further reference to the case of Lord Dundonald, who was the general officer commanding in Canada in 1904. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then prime minister of Canada, spoke in the debate that arose out of this case and I should like to quote his words, as reported in column 5533 of Hansard of June 24, 1904 as follows:
You will see in this but one more of the numerous contests for supremacy between the military power and the civil power which have taken place in England and in all British countries for many ages back. In England, sir, and in all British countries, and indeed in all civilized countries, these contests have taken place, but with this difference, however, that in all countries except England and British possessions, this contest invariably

Committee on Defence Expenditure terminated by the civil power being crushed by the military power; whereas in England and in British countries, countries that enjoy British laws the contest was decided once for all in favour of the civil power and of civil liberty. But though this contest was decided more than 100 years ago, still it is now and then revived by the military power.
I suggest that in the publication of this report and its distribution to the army, and in this reference to the Auditor General's report, there is an indication that some people are not considering parliament in respect to its relationship to the military power of this country. We all know that under British practice it is strictly forbidden for any member of the high command to comment on any political question or upon the happenings in parliament. I am informed by a good authority that on one occasion since 1945 a top ranking commander in the British army made a slight reference to the happenings in parliament and political developments, and was called immediately before the Prime Minister of Great Britain and told that that sort of thing was just not done.
I should like to refer again to what occurred in the house in 1904 and I quote from columns 4624 and 4626 of Hansard of June 10, 1904, where Mr. Henri Bourassa, speaking on the same Lord Dundonald matter, had this to say:
I think it is well that we should understand exactly the point at issue, not only before the house, but before the country. That point is whether the general officer commanding the militia of Canada is a servant of the government or not. If he is not a servant of the government, I quite accept the conclusion of hon. gentlemen opposite and say that he should not be interfered with by politicians. But, if it is acknowledged, as I always thought it was acknowledged, that he is a servant of the government, that he is appointed and paid by the government and therefore must report to the minister-who is responsible to the house-before stating anything to the country, then, I think the course of Lord Dundonald is absolutely indefensible.
But so long as this general officer commanding is in the position of any other public servant, he is bound to be silent, bound to do what would be the duty of any officer in his position in any civilized country.
Those remarks are strictly in accord with British tradition as to the relationship between parliament and the military power. Before concluding I should like to deal with the propriety of the Prime Minister tabling the letter written by the chief of the general staff, which has tended to have some influence on the public mind with regard to this Currie report and the consequential debate in parliament. I refer again to the debate that occurred in the Lord Dundonald case. There was another interesting aspect to that case which I think has a direct bearing upon the Prime Minister's action in tabling the communique from the chief of the general


staff. Lord Dundonald had submitted a report, and it was argued by some that the minister of militia should have tabled the report. In that debate the then prime minister of Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier-I know hon. members on the other side hold his memory in greatest respect-quoted from Todd, that great parliamentary authority of Great Britain. He gave a series of quotations, but I should like to read only one or two. I refer hon. members to column 5541 of Hansard of June 4, 1904, where the then prime minister quotes Todd as follows:
The system of laying upon the table of the house reports from officers addressed to particular departments of the executive government is most objectionable.
He then went on to quote Disraeli who had spoken in the British house on the question of the tabling of correspondence or reports by officers addressed to executive members of parliament.
This is what Laurier quotes Disraeli as saying:
There have been cases in which reports of a confidential character from officers of the government have been laid upon the table of the house, to prepare the public mind, and also that of parliament, to consent to some large measure, or perhaps some considerable vote of public money; but generally I think it is a course which the house ought not to sanction.
These are opinions from high authorities which I think indicate some grounds for saying that we consider it improper for reports to be tabled in that way. If the chief of the general staff wanted the matter brought to the attention of the house he had the right to bring it to the attention of his minister or the Prime Minister, and then it would be the duty of the political executive to bring the matter to the attention of the house.
I mention my objections to these things at this time because I find that the newspapers of the country have shown considerable interest through their comments, and newspapers do not comment on things of this sort unless they realize that a principle is at stake or that a large number of people are interested. I also find that quite a number of people are most concerned about this development. I am not suggesting that at this stage it is a serious one, but I do think it is a development that should be nipped in the bud by the Prime Minister and the minister of the department concerned.
This is a democracy; and in our opinion if we are going to maintain it as a democracy parliament and the civil power should always remain supreme. Democracy on occasions, Mr. Speaker, has to be defended on the field of battle. However, its ultimate and final defence rests in the hearts and hands of those

who live in the cottages of our land. I am sure all members of the house will agree with me when I say that their front-line trench is parliament.

Mr. Speaker, in beginning my remarks I should like to say a word to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) because he commenced proceedings this evening by admitting that the point of order raised this afternoon was not well taken and that Sergeant Young actually has applied for parole. I would think the word "parole" would have a great attraction for the Minister of Justice and the other members of the government, because if there is anything they need it is parole from their present responsibilities. I am glad to see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) back in the house. I am also glad to say that, in spite of fairly strong political differences and probably harsh words back and forth in the house, personally we have remained quite friendly. I think that is one of the good things about this chamber.
I was sorry for the minister tonight because he was, in the words of my leader this afternoon, in the position of trying to explain the unexplainable. That of course is not novel for Liberal speakers during the past few years. They have had quite a number of unexplainable things to try to explain. I should like to comment on some of the matters the minister raised. While he was speaking I scribbled away fairly rapidly, but it may be that I missed some. However, I have a number of notes that cover most of them.
One of the first things he said was that the red herrings are beginning to smell, referring to a certain amount of comment that has come from this side of the house with respect to the red herrings the government has been attempting to drag across the Currie report. All I can say is that the minister's olfactory senses cannot be very keen or he would have recognized some time ago that the red herring was beginning to smell. The biggest red herring that has been brought into the debate so far is the attempt to make out that the most important issue before us is how the C.C.F. got possession of a draft copy of the report. That is the chief red herring that has been introduced into the debate.
It is beyond me why the members of the government would think that was a matter which the general public of the country were going to look upon as being very important, compared with the budget of $2 billion being spent on defence with which this debate is supposed to be dealing, to a considerable extent, in that we are talking about the
Committee on Defence Expenditure setting up of a defence expenditure committee. I do not understand why the government would think a red herring of that sort would have very much effect so far as the general public are concerned. That is certainly the smelliest of all the smelly red herrings that have been introduced. I am not, however, going to enter into the Liberal-C.C.F. argument that has been going on with respect to whether an extremely serious offence was committed when the C.C.F. got hold of a draft copy of the report. I think I can quite readily leave that to my friends of the C.C.F.
The minister also said that the only person who had dealt with parts II, III and IV of the report-the ones containing the recommendations-was himself. As a matter of fact, as I tried to point out to him by an interjection during his speech, I dealt with those parts when speaking on this matter before Christmas, at the time the Currie report was first tabled in the house. I dealt particularly with one recommendation which I think is extremely good, namely that a pilot plant or company should be set up so far as the works services are concerned. I recommended at that time, and I recommend now, that pilot companies, pilot battalions, pilot batteries and so forth be set up for all the various branches of the army and the other defence services, so people can see how things should be done properly and how they can be done properly, and then can go back to their own units and apply what they have learned.
I pointed out at that time that from my reading of history that was one of the chief strengths of the German army and one of the reasons they were able to train as good an army as they did in a relatively short period before the last war. That is one of the recommendations I dealt with at some length before Christmas, and I emphasize it again now because I think it is so important. Any attempt the minister may have been trying to make to represent that the members on this side of the house are not interested in the recommendations, that all we are interested in is the first part of the report which blisters the government, is a complete failure. We are even more interested in the latter parts of the report and the recommendations contained therein than in the first part, and we are particularly interested that those recommendations be put into effect.
I shall come back to that matter later. Certainly if the recommendations are to be put into effect it is absolutely useless to place them before the defence expenditure committee. The very name of the committee

He finally admits for the first time that everything is not perfect, and it is the very first time.
The next matter the minister dealt with was the fact that complaints had been made from this side of the house to the effect that the rapid demobilization which took place following the war had been responsible for the lack of personnel in the army works services, and that therefore the policy of the government was responsible for the present mess at Petawawa and elsewhere. I think he quoted the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and another hon. member in that regard. The minister said that rapid demobilization on the contrary had contributed greatly to the "prosperity of the country"; that is the note I made. He said it would have caused a great deal of disgruntlement amongst servicemen if it had not taken place. I agree with that; but what happened was that a great number of people who did not want to be demobilized were demobilized against their will, the very people who had administrative experience, who could have trained the other members of these works companies and other administrative people throughout the army.
I also spoke on this matter before Christmas and I do not like to repeat what I said then, but apparently the minister paid no attention to what I said at that time, and to what others said. Following the war the Department of National Defence followed the policy of getting out of the army all of the older officers who had had experience before the war in the peacetime administration of the army, the older N.C.O.'s and so on. A very considerable number of those people were retired years before their normal time for pension.
As a result of that policy of retiring these people-I think the idea was that by getting rid of the older fellows they could make room for younger fellows and then keep promoting them more rapidly, and so on-nearly all the men who had any amount of administrative and accounting experience and so on were let out. That was particularly true with those who had served in the Canadian army before the war. They were let out after the war, and we started with a group of green people. A great many had no experience along administrative and accounting lines.

Their experience during the war had been fighting experience; it was not administrative experience. It is no wonder they did not do a good job, and took a long time to learn the job.
So I place the responsibility for this situation which has developed at Petawawa, and generally as far as administration is concerned, squarely on the shoulders of this government, because of the policy they followed after the war of getting rid of people who did have administrative experience, accounting experience and so on.
The minister went on to say something about the obsolescence or otherwise of the F-86E Sabre. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very technical matter and there is not very much use of either the minister or myself, or any other member, making assertions about it.
I personally hope very much that what the minister said was correct, that the P-86E Sabre is the best fighter in production. Unfortunately I must point out that the United States jet fighter pilots who have come back from Korea have not said that. It is useless for the minister and myself to get into an argument on the matter because I know that neither he nor I have the technical knowledge to know what we are talking about. We are just taking assertions from this, that or the other person. In any event I will say no more about that particular matter.
The minister next asked why should we refer or why are we referring the Currie report to the committee. He said there were a lot of reasons which perhaps had not been mentioned. The first reason was to secure simplification in regard to the filling of posts. Goodness gracious, how can referring this report to the committee do anything in the world in regard to simplification as far as filling posts is concerned? The committee cannot do anything about that. All the committee can do is to listen to the recommendations from Mr. Currie or others, recommendations which he has already made to the government.
Once more this is one of the things which can only have any effect if the government takes it up and gets some good personnel managers on the job, gets them to work and gets posts filled as a result. Referring it to the committee is only going to delay getting personnel on the job, and the determination of what is required in posts in the army works services or other branches. The minister gave a second reason, but he wandered around and I really did not gather enough about it to comment.
Next was the question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). In reply
Committee on Defence Expenditure to that question the minister said that 1,100 odd reports from the auditors of his own department had been made. On further questioning, as I understood him, he said he had read none of those reports. Was that correct? He had not read a single one of those 1,100 reports submitted by his own inspecting officers or auditors, some of which reports are referred to in the Currie report.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that many of the present troubles in the Department of National Defence might have been prevented if the minister had read those reports. I think this was one of the -most significant admissions the Minister of National Defence has yet made in this house. I referred to one a while ago, that everything was not perfect. Now this is a more significant admission because it shows clearly that the breakdown of administration which took place in his department was the result of not paying any attention to the inspection and auditing system which they had. Under any reasonable system at all I should say the minister would have had the more important of these auditors' reports brought to his attention. At the very least, Mr. Speaker, if the administrative set-up in the department had been running at all properly, a digest of these auditors' reports, and of the things which they showed were wrong, would have been placed before the minister every month or every two weeks, or at some such stated periods. Then, they having been brought to his attention, he could have taken some effective action to correct them. As the situation was, none of these 1,100 irregularities which the auditors reported was ever brought to the attention of the minister. Under those circumstances how could you expect any corrective action to be taken?

Committee on Defence Expenditure in and listen only to government members, I am sure would have been greatly perturbed and puzzled as to what was the motion before the house. We of course are on a motion to set up a committee to investigate defence expenditure, the same sort of committee that we had for this purpose last year. I think the terms of reference are exactly the same. To that motion the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) moved an amendment. The amendment directs the committee, when set up, to first consider the Currie report.
As has been abundantly shown by all those who have spoken on this side of the house,
I think that report speaks for itself. I can think of nothing less valuable than to have the committee on defence expenditure spend its time, in effect, in investigating the investigator. That is what we would be doing, and that is all the defence expenditure committee can and will do if it is turned loose on this Currie report. We shall be investigating the investigator, the very man the Minister of National Defence and this government appointed for the purpose of investigating the irregularities which had taken place at Petawawa, who spent months in doing that, and who turned in what I think everyone will admit was an absolutely splendid report.
The reason for the tactics of the government in moving this amendment, Mr. Speaker, seems to be quite clear. I do not think there is much doubt about it. The first thing they hope to accomplish by doing that is this: By having the committee go minutely over the Currie report, clause by clause, their objective is to try to cast some doubt on some of the items which are contained in it and, at the same time, by spending weeks in that procedure, to smother the whole report in words. As a matter of fact, that is the technique which was employed so effectively on many occasions by their late leader, Mr. Mackenzie King: smother the thing in words. That seems to be what they are going to try to do in the committee on defence expenditure with regard to this report.
A second and probably much more important purpose would be served, as far as the government is concerned, in moving this amendment, and it is this. As a result of considering the Currie report the committee would not have time to investigate the much more important matters on which it should be engaged. Those matters are the expenditures, by this time something over $3 billion, on our rearmament. How much more than $3 billion it is, I do not know. It certainly must be considerably more than


that by this time because the committee's work starts back when the Korean war began in 1950.
What happened last year in the committee on defence expenditure I think presents a reasonable parallel with what happened here in the house this year with regard to this amendment moved by the minister. I think probably the- results which were achieved last year in the committee by the tactics followed there suggested the present course to the government and constitute the reason they have adopted it. Last year in the defence expenditure committee I made a motion that the committee should investigate the situation which had developed at Petawawa, but the government would not hear of it. Oh, no; there was no chance at all. It was sub judice. Everything was wrong with that idea.
In the committee we talked about the matter for some time. The government was in this position, I think. They did not want a vote on the issue directly. They thought it would look bad through the country to refuse to have the committee investigate Petawawa, so the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) rose and moved an amendment to that motion. The amendment was in this form:
That all the words after "that" be struck out-
And "that" was the first word in my motion. It can therefore be seen that the idea was to slaughter my motion completely.
I may say that this was on April 29, 1952. The amendment continues:
-and the following substituted therefor:
That pursuant to the terms of reference of this committee evidence be taken from competent witnesses dealing with the administrative procedures laid down by the Department of National Defence for the receipt, stockkeeping, issue and accounting of stores, material and equipment at military camps and establishments and in particular the steps taken to prevent, discover and eliminate the loss, misuse or wastage of government property of every kind and that the committee thereafter consider what further steps, if any, should be taken.
Of course that amendment was adopted by the Liberal majority of two to one on the committee. Those are all exceedingly high-sounding words. It sounded as though this were going to be a terrific committee, and as though they were going to carry on a terrific investigation. But in actual fact, Mr. Speaker, here is what it accomplished. It accomplished the purpose of keeping the committee occupied, for half of its entire sittings, with a mass of detail on hundreds of sheets of paper-and they were piled up to a considerable height-which contained lists of losses by fire, theft and other irregularities in the navy, the army and the air force, including items of $2.50, $3.69 and so

forth. We were expected to go through- and we did so as far as two of the services were concerned-these long lists, item by item, with an explanation on the side as to how this loss of $2.50 had taken place, and so on. What was accomplished by all that was this. Instead of doing the work which it was appointed to do; instead of doing the work it should have done; instead of doing the work that it was necessary should be done for the welfare of this country, that committee was smothered with this great mass of unimportant details which we had not asked for and which was pushed on top of us.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, an analysis of the meetings of that committee. The committee met first, for organizational purposes, on April 8. It was just an organization meeting. Following that meeting we had seventeen working sessions. Mark you, Mr. Chairman, this important committee held its first working session on April 22. It took all that time for the government to get around to the point of even getting the committee started, before they started to smother it. We started on April 22 and we finished on June 17 having, as I say, held seventeen working sessions, two of them on the last day we sat.
In order that there will be no mistake, the last working day we sat was June 12. We had two sessions, morning and afternoon. On June 17 we had a closed session to consider the report, which was presented to us in mimeographed form. It had been prepared by the chairman or somebody else, I do not know whom, but there it was in front of us, and they said: "There is your report." That is the great committee to which members on that side of the house will refer and say: "The committee on defence expenditure considered this, and they did not find anything wrong. The committee on defence expenditure did not find anything wrong with this particular matter. They did not turn in any adverse report on it." Mr. Speaker, do you think that any report brought in on a mimeographed sheet of paper by the chairman of the committee and presented to the members of the committee was going to be critical of anything the department had done? Why, the thing is unthinkable.

It seems to me that what the people of Canada are interested in is in seeing that value is received for the money spent on defence. That is the main thing that the people of Canada want at the present time. I do not think any Canadian grudges one cent or one dollar which is spent effectively for the defence effort. I emphasize the word "effectively" because the people of this country almost universally do grudge and complain bitterly about the money which is taken from them and wasted, as far as the defence effort is concerned, and which contributes to the inefficiency which has been displayed up to date in regard to our rearmament effort and defence spending generally.
At the present time people are making up their income tax returns. Those people are not too interested in how the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) got hold of an unauthorized copy or a draft copy of the Currie report. They are not too interested in that or in the other extraneous matters which have been brought up here, the red herrings which have been referred to. What they are interested in, and what they are concerned about is how their dollars are being spent for defence. They are very interested in that; and a task which the defence expenditure committee can do for them is to


determine whether these dollars are being properly and effectively spent in at least some ways in the defence department. Under the course followed by the government that committee is going to be prevented from discovering that.
The government, as I mentioned before, has attempted to make this disappearance of a draft copy a major question. The major effort on their part is to distract attention from the really important questions posed by the Currie report. The important criticism of the government in the Currie report is not the various details which the minister has spoken about. It is the general breakdown in administration which has taken place within the Department of National Defence, the cost of which Mr. Currie has said cannot even be estimated, and which is certainly very much greater than the value of the articles which were stolen or otherwise made away with.
I have comments here on speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the other Liberal members who have spoken in this debate. I see that I have not time to deal with them all. I would sum up all the speeches which have been made by Liberal members in defence of the government as far as the Currie report is concerned in this way. They were a confused mass of irrelevancies, and they exhibited a complete failure to meet the important criticisms to which I have referred, which are either definitely made or implied in the Currie report and also in the report of the Auditor General.
The criticisms which are either made or implied in these reports are criticisms which we on this side of the house have made here in the past three or four years. Year after year we have been telling the Minister of National Defence that things are not going well this way, or that they are not going well that way; that his general administrative set-up in the Department of National Defence headquarters is staff-heavy; that there is too much red tape; that in some places he has too much staff and in other places he has not enough; that his department is badly organized.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) urged that a firm of efficiency experts should be brought in to make recommendations to the minister as to how the civilian or administrative part of his department could be reorganized so that he would have a more effective and better working department, but the minister has always pooh-poohed the idea. He has said, "The department does not need an efficiency experu They are small potatoes, so far as

we are concerned". According to the minister, only small concerns call in efficiency experts today. Well, I venture to say that if he had called one in three years ago the government would not be in the position they are today with regard to the Currie report.
